# Session 2: Foundations of probability and statistics

In this practical, you will explore the dataset for your specialisation, choose a variable and explain what you learn from the results. You are welcome to discuss your work with other students, but you must submit it individually or in pairs.

At each stage, find the relevant R code block in Session 2, copy it into the chunk provided and adapt it to your dataset. Any extra guidance you need is included in this R Markdown document, so there is no need to memorise every command.

Before running a piece of code, take a moment to predict what it will produce. Afterwards, compare the result with your prediction and try to explain any differences.

Today's guiding question is: **What can we learn from our dataset, and how far can we take our conclusions?**

| Stage |
|---|
| A. Open the document and load your dataset |
| B. Ask a question and choose a variable |
| C. Explore the distribution and its centre |
| D. Describe the spread |
| E. Calculate an observed proportion |
| F. Explore a normal model |
| G. Draw conclusions and check your document |

## A. Getting started

### Set up your workspace
1. Extract the practical's ZIP archive into your workspace, for example `H:\AnalyseDonnees\Session2`. Open the `.Rmd` file in RStudio. Select **Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location** to set the working directory to the folder containing the file.
2. Rename your copy `Session2_SURNAME_Firstname.Rmd` if you are working individually, or `Session2_SURNAME1_Firstname1_SURNAME2_Firstname2.Rmd` if you are working in a pair.
3. Keep the `data` folder **in the same folder as the R Markdown document**. Also open the [Session 2 course page](https://flo-unige.github.io/analyse-donnees-statistiques/cours/session-02/index-en-r.html) in your browser. You will reuse the water quality examples from the course, adapting them to work with your own dataset.

To run an R chunk, click its green triangle. To run a line or selection, press **Ctrl + Enter**. Write your answers in the Markdown sections, outside the R chunks. Once you have completed the work, use **Knit** to produce an HTML version with your results and plots.

## C. Explore the distribution and its centre

### What do your data look like?

A **histogram** groups values into intervals called bins. Before drawing one, think about what you might see: will the countries have similar values, or will they differ widely?

Find the course block that draws a histogram and copy it below.

Before running it, identify everything specific to the water quality example: the name of the object holding the values, the units, the text labels and the axis settings. What needs to change for the plot to describe your countries and use your variables correctly?

**Tips for adjusting the plot:**
- `breaks` sets the bin edges. A single number, such as `breaks=10`, is only a suggestion to R. To get exactly 10 bins of equal width, use `bin_edges <- seq(min(my_series), max(my_series), length.out = 11)`, then `breaks = bin_edges`. Replace `my_series` with the name chosen in B. For 20 bins, you need 21 edges.
- Keep `right = FALSE` and add `include.lowest = TRUE`. Each bin includes its left edge, and the maximum value is still included in the last bin. Use `freq = TRUE` to display counts.
- The course code removes the vertical axis with `yaxt = "n"`, then sets the tick marks using `axis(2, at = 0:3)`. You can remove both settings and let R choose the ticks.
- Try changing the other arguments to understand what they do and create a plot that suits your variable.

Compare the plots with 10 and 20 bins, then keep the one that makes the distribution easier to read.

## F. Explore a normal model

### Build a curve on your variable's scale

A **normal distribution** is a symmetric, bell-shaped model. Its mean `mu` sets its centre, and its standard deviation `sigma` determines its spread.

We will use your descriptive summaries to draw a curve on the same scale as your variable. This does not mean that the variable follows a normal distribution. You may well conclude that the model is a poor fit.

To draw this curve, we need at least two measurements and a strictly positive standard deviation. If all your values are identical, discuss your choice of variable with me.

---

Find the course block that plots a normal distribution and shades an interval. We will use your descriptive summaries to build a curve on your variable's scale.

Before editing the block, identify the mean, standard deviation, interval bounds, text labels and axis limits set for the water quality example. Which of these depend on the variable being studied?

The plotting syntax is new, so here is some guidance to help you understand it. **Replace the example names `my_series` and `descriptive_std` with the names of your own objects.**

To set the parameters and define an interval extending one standard deviation on either side of the mean, replace the parameter definitions from the course with:

```r
mu <- mean(my_series)
sigma <- descriptive_std
lower_bound <- mu - sigma
upper_bound <- mu + sigma
```

`seq` creates evenly spaced values for drawing the curve. For the shaded interval, use:

```r
interval <- seq(lower_bound, upper_bound, length.out = 200)
```

`pnorm` gives the probability of a value being less than or equal to a given bound under the model. We calculate the following difference:

```r
probability <- pnorm(upper_bound, mu, sigma) - pnorm(lower_bound, mu, sigma)
```

In `polygon`, also replace `c(4, interval, 6)` with `c(lower_bound, interval, upper_bound)`. Keep the instructions that draw the curve, then adapt the titles, units and legend labels. In `legend`, you can use `sprintf("Selected interval: %.1f %%", 100 * probability)` for the shaded area and `sprintf("Model centre: %.2f", mu)` for the centre line.

The `ylim` argument sets the vertical limits. Remove it to let R adjust the axis to your scale. If you remove arguments, check the remaining commas and parentheses to avoid syntax errors.

**Find it in the [Session 2 R course](https://flo-unige.github.io/analyse-donnees-statistiques/cours/session-02/index-en-r.html#exemple-2-2-loi-normale):** "The normal distribution", block `exemple-2-2-loi-normale`.
